hints: Find the attacked piece and the piece that attacks it.
A bishop can only go to squares on its own diagonals. For each square ask two questions: does Black attack it, and if so, does White defend it?
The four squares down the long diagonal toward your own side are still attacked by Black's bishop, but White defends each of them.
items.explain: The bishop on d5 can be taken for free, because nothing defends it. Be4, Bf3, Bg2 and Bh1 stay on the same diagonal as the black bishop, so it can still take there, but each square is defended (by the d3 pawn, the queen or the king), so the worst case is a trade of bishops. Each leaves nothing else loose.

hints: Which piece attacks the knight? Compare its counting value with the knight's.
A queen that takes a defended knight loses more than it wins, so any defender is enough here.
A pawn can defend the knight directly, and so can a piece that gets onto its file, rank or diagonal.
items.explain: The queen has a higher counting value than the knight (9 and 3), so once the knight has a defender, taking it would cost White the queen for a knight. Each of Rc8, b6, Qc6, Qc7, Qc8 and e6 adds a defender and leaves nothing else loose.
